title: "GitHub Desktop Setup"
---

## GitHub Desktop: Version Control Without the Command Line

GitHub Desktop is a free application that lets you commit and push with a visual interface instead of typing git commands. It is **optional**. VS Code's Source Control panel does the same job in the window you are already in.

It does **not** create your repository. Your workspace comes from the [course template](https://github.com/AURA-Lab-SIUE/v2v-workspace), already public and already on GitHub. GitHub Desktop is only a way to send your weekly work to it.

**Time needed:** 10 minutes

---

## Step 1: Download and Install

1. Visit [desktop.github.com](https://desktop.github.com/)
2. Download the installer for your operating system (Windows or Mac)
3. Run the installer; it requires no special configuration
4. When prompted, sign in with your GitHub account (the one you created in Week 1)

---

## Step 2: Add Your Workspace to GitHub Desktop

Your workspace repository already exists: you created it from the template and cloned it into VS Code. GitHub Desktop only needs to be pointed at that folder.

1. Open GitHub Desktop
2. Click **File > Add Local Repository**
3. Navigate to your cloned workspace folder and select it
4. You should now see your workspace files listed in the "Changes" tab

Do not use **File > New Repository**. That makes a second, unconnected repository, and your work would stop matching the URL you submitted.

---

## Step 3: Make Your First Commit

A **commit** is a snapshot of your work at a specific point in time. Think of it as saving a version.

1. In GitHub Desktop, you should see all your workspace files listed as "Changes"
2. In the **Summary** field at the bottom left, type: `Initial workspace setup`
3. Click **Commit to main**
4. Your files are now tracked by git

---

## Step 4: Push to GitHub

Your repository is already on GitHub, and already public, because it came from the template. You never publish it a second time.

1. Click **Push origin** in the top bar
2. Refresh your repository page on github.com, and your commit is there
3. Your workspace lives at `https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/mc451-workspace`

---

## Weekly Workflow: Push Your Journal

After writing each journal entry in VS Code:

1. Open GitHub Desktop; it will automatically detect the new/changed files
2. Review the changes in the "Changes" tab (you should see your new journal entry)
3. Type a commit message: `Week 3 journal` (or similar)
4. Click **Commit to main**
5. Click **Push origin** in the top bar

Your journal entry is now on GitHub. Your instructor can see your commit history, and you are building a visible record of consistent work.

---

## Key Vocabulary

| Term | What It Means |
|------|--------------|
| **Repository (repo)** | A folder tracked by git; it knows every change you have made |
| **Commit** | A saved snapshot of your work with a message describing what changed |
| **Push** | Upload your commits to GitHub so they are visible online |
| **Pull** | Download changes from GitHub to your local machine (used when collaborating) |
| **Branch** | A parallel version of your repository (you will use `main` for this course) |

---

## Troubleshooting

**"Repository not found" when publishing**
Make sure you are signed into the correct GitHub account in GitHub Desktop (File > Options > Accounts).

**Changes not showing up**
GitHub Desktop only tracks files inside the repository folder. Make sure your journal entries are saved inside your course workspace folder, not somewhere else.

**"Merge conflict" error**
This happens if you edited a file on GitHub.com and also locally. For this course, always edit locally in VS Code and push, never edit directly on GitHub.com.

**Large files warning**
Git works best with text files. Do not commit large data files (CSVs over 50MB, images, PDFs) to your workspace repository. Keep those in your `04_Resources/` folder locally but add them to `.gitignore`.
